title: The bow in the clouds (Genesis 8–9)
hook: after the flood, God's promise with every living thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Noah builds: a ship under a clear sky, and a man who did all things God commanded. Your line was build anyway.

A hundred and fifty days, the water rules the earth. Then it begins to fall. The ark grounds on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven, which flies back and forth. Then a dove, which finds nowhere to land and comes back to his hand. He waits seven days and sends her again, and at evening she returns with an olive leaf in her beak. Seven days more, and she doesn't come back at all. A dove with an olive branch still turns up on flags and posters as a sign of peace. But the story isn't finished when the ground dries.
screen: `A RAVEN, BACK AND FORTH.` → `A DOVE WITH AN OLIVE LEAF.` → `THEN SHE DOESN'T COME BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, more than a contract, closer to a family bond. God promised one to Noah before the flood; here it is made. Second, who's in it: Noah, his sons, their children after them, and, the text keeps saying, every living creature, birds, cattle, beasts of the earth. The animals are partners in a promise. Third, what's promised: never again will a flood destroy the earth. And the sign, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth." The Hebrew word for bow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow. Some readers picture God hanging up the weapon, pointed away from the earth; the text doesn't spell that out. But the text is clear about who the sign is for: when the bow appears, God says, I will remember. The reminder is for God. Fourth, why the Church cares. The Catechism places this covenant within God's plan of salvation, and says it stays in force for the nations until the gospel is proclaimed to the whole world. It closes a week that began with a lonely man in a garden: a serpent's question, a call into the trees, the first good news, a brother's blood, an ark, and now color across the sky.
screen: `BERIT: A BINDING PROMISE.` · `EVERY LIVING CREATURE IS IN IT.` · `A BOW HUNG IN THE CLOUDS.` · `THE REMINDER IS FOR GOD.` · then, large: `I WILL REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: If you can see a window, look out of it now; if not, picture the last sky you noticed, and let your eyes rest on whatever color is there. Then think of every creature under that same sky, birds, a neighbor's dog, a fish you'll never see, a stranger across the world, all inside one promise in the story. If you pray, give thanks for them.
Covenant. Berit in Hebrew: a binding promise. After the flood, God makes one with Noah and every living creature, and sets a bow in the clouds as its sign.
Your line: a promise to every creature. The birds and the beasts are in it too. That's the week.

howItsDone: The Church reads God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:8–15) on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, and the Catechism describes it as God's covenant with all the nations.

notes: Week end (days 337–343): the look-back sits at the end of the teach. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims Genesis 9:13 quoted from memory; confirm.
'First time in Genesis in full': berit first appears at 6:18 (promised to Noah) and is established in 9:9–17. Confirm the phrasing.
The bow as a warrior's bow hung up is an interpretive image; the script says so. Confirm.

The dove's flights (8:8–12): first returns with nothing, second with an olive leaf, third doesn't return. The raven 'went forth and did not return' in the Douay-Rheims (Vulgate) versus 'to and fro' in the Hebrew; the script says 'flies back and forth'. Confirm.
CCC 56–58 (covenant with Noah, in force while the nations last), CCC 71. Paraphrased; confirm. howItsDone: Genesis 9:8–15 is the first reading for Lent I, Year B; confirm.
